instructions:
You are an auditor checking one checklist item against the regulatory clause it claims to come from. Start
from the ITEM: read it, then look in the clause for each thing the item asks for.

A clause may hold several separate obligations, each turned into its own item. Judge the item against the
part of the clause it covers (given as COVERS), not against the whole clause. But that part must be a whole
obligation: if a condition, number, frequency or qualifier that belongs to the same obligation is left out,
of the item or of the COVERS span, it counts as omitted.

Judge only what the item's own words say. Do not read the clause back into the item: a condition, trigger,
timing or qualifier that is in the clause but not in the item is omitted, even if it seems implied or obvious.
A trigger such as "if", "where ... is required", "when" or "before" is part of the obligation; an item that
leaves it out turns a conditional duty into an unconditional one, which is stricter, or changes its timing.

Answer every question strictly:
- required_by_clause: does the clause require what the item asks for (true/false)?
- item_adds: anything the item asks for that the clause does not say (empty string if nothing).
- item_omits: anything belonging to the covered obligation that the item leaves out, including conditions,
  numbers and frequencies (empty string if nothing). Other, separate obligations of the clause are not
  omissions.
- strictness: "same", "stricter" (the item demands more than the clause) or "looser" (less).
- plant_types_ok: is the clause applicable to every listed plant type (true/false)?
- strength_ok: does the item's strength (mandatory / recommended / optional) match the clause's wording
  (shall/must = mandatory, should = recommended, may = optional) (true/false)?
- verdict: "correct" only if required_by_clause and plant_types_ok and strength_ok are true, strictness is
  "same", and item_adds and item_omits are empty; otherwise "incorrect".
- reason: one or two sentences.

ITEM: Production and control operations are clearly defined and carried out under GMP.
Strength: recommended
Plant types: INJ, LIQ, OSD, SEMI
COVERS: Production and control operations are clearly specified and Good Manufacturing Practice adopted

Source: EU - Part I Chapter 1 Pharmaceutical Quality System
Applies to plant types: INJ, LIQ, OSD, SEMI
Clause 1.4:
1.4 A Pharmaceutical Quality System appropriate for the manufacture of medicinal products should ensure that: (i) Product realisation is achieved by designing, planning, implementing, maintaining and continuously improving a system that allows the consistent delivery of products with appropriate quality attributes; (ii) Product and process knowledge is managed throughout all lifecycle stages; (iii) Medicinal products are designed and developed in a way that takes account of the requirements of Good Manufacturing Practice; (iv) Production and control operations are clearly specified and Good Manufacturing Practice adopted; (v) Managerial responsibilities are clearly specified; (vi) Arrangements are made for the manufacture, supply and use of the correct starting and packaging materials, the selection and monitoring of suppliers and for verifying that each delivery is from the approved supply chain; (vii) Processes are in place to assure the management of outsourced activities. (viii) A state of control is established and maintained by developing and using effective monitoring and control systems for process performance and product quality. (ix) The results of product and processes monitoring are taken into account in batch release, in the investigation of deviations, and, with a view to taking preventive action to avoid potential deviations occurring in the future. (x) All necessary controls on intermediate products, and any other in-process controls and validations are carried out; (xi) Continual improvement is facilitated through the implementation of quality improvements appropriate to the current level of process and product knowledge. (xii) Arrangements are in place for the prospective evaluation of planned changes and their approval prior to implementation taking into account regulatory notification and approval where required; (xiii) After implementation of any change, an evaluation is undertaken to confirm the quality objectives were achieved and that there was no unintended deleterious impact on product quality; (xiv) An appropriate level of root cause analysis should be applied during the investigation of deviations, suspected product defects and other problems.
